title: Map: yt-transcript — a Node CLI for YouTube transcripts
description:
## Destination

A **spec ticket** describing the `yt-transcript` Node CLI — invocation, Markdown output contract, catalog, and playlist behaviour — together with `CONTEXT.md`, any ADRs, and the agent procedure doc, such that **one implementer session** can build it end to end.

## Notes

**Domain:** turning YouTube videos the user has no time to watch into Markdown transcripts usable as agent input or reference material. Explicitly **not** summaries.

**Skills every session should consult:** `grilling` and `domain-modeling`. Write `CONTEXT.md` lazily and inline as terms resolve; offer ADRs only for decisions that are hard to reverse, surprising, and the result of a real trade-off.

### Settled during charting — do NOT re-ask the user

- **Shape:** a Node.js application, run locally via `npx` (not published to npm; structured so publishing stays a later option). Command name: `yt-transcript`.
- **No PowerShell.** `Get-Transcript.ps1` is retired; there is no `scripts/` folder. The repo *is* the application — standard Node layout.
- **Fetching (settled, see Decisions):** the CLI spawns the **`yt-dlp` binary** as a child process, preflight-checking for it on PATH and failing with a clear, actionable message if absent. Always pass **`--js-runtimes node`** — it costs nothing, silences the deprecation warning, and keeps the pipeline working if subtitles ever do start requiring a JS runtime. Pure-JS fetching was investigated and **rejected as not durable**; do not re-open it. Full evidence: `archive/research/yt-dlp-js-runtime-and-pure-js-paths.md`.
- **Input:** accepts a YouTube URL **or** a bare video id. Must tolerate `youtube.com/watch?v=`, `youtu.be/`, `/shorts/`, and trailing `?si=` / `&t=` junk.
- **Output:** one Markdown file per video in a **flat** `transcripts/` directory, named in kebab-case from the video title.
- **Frontmatter (settled, see Decisions):** exactly seven keys in fixed order — `title`, `url`, `channel`, `duration`, `upload_date`, `fetched`, `subtitles` (`manual` | `auto`). No separate `video_id` — the URL carries it.
- **Subtitles:** prefer manually-authored subtitles, fall back to auto-generated; record which was used. Default language `en`, overridable.
- **Paragraphing (settled, see Decisions):** break at the next **sentence end** once the paragraph reaches **100 words**; `PARAGRAPH_MIN_WORDS = 100`, hard-coded, not a flag. **Timing is not used at all** — cue gaps are exactly 0.000s in every sample, so no pause threshold can fire, and word-level timing proved speaker-dependent. Do not re-open the 2.0s/0.8s pause idea. The sentence signal is YouTube's own ASR punctuation.
- **Catalog (settled, see Decisions):** `transcripts/README.md`, a Markdown table **derived** from the transcript files' frontmatter so it cannot drift, rebuilt by full rescan.
- **Single entry point.** No script invoking another script; one CLI with flags/subcommands.
- **`package.json` is required** with `"type": "module"` and `"engines": { "node": ">=22" }` — v22 is yt-dlp's floor for `--js-runtimes node`, and this machine runs v24. The cleaner currently relies on Node's ESM auto-detection, and `fnm --use-on-cd` makes the active Node version variable by design. Specify this; it is not a ticket.
- **Defence in depth:** when spawning `yt-dlp`, strip any `fnm_multishells` entries from the child process PATH. The root cause is fixed on this machine, but the guard keeps the tool portable.
- **Existing artifacts:** 7 `.vtt` files and their `_cleaned.txt` siblings sit at the repo root, plus strays (an `.srt`, a `-transcript.txt`, a file whose name begins with `--`). The cleaned text is migrated into `transcripts/` with real titles; the `.vtt` intermediates are deleted as regenerable. This is hand-off execution, not a decision.

### Tracker mechanics (verified against br 0.6.0)

- Use `--description-file`, **never** `-d/--description` — a `"` in the text breaks shell quoting and spills a positional argument.
- Colons in labels are accepted (`wayfinder:map`).
- `--parent` creates hierarchy but does **not** block. Blocking is `br dep add <issue> <depends-on>` (default type `blocks`).
- **Frontier query:** `br ready --json`. Blocked work: `br blocked --json`.
- Run `br sync --flush-only` after mutations. **This repo IS under git** (branch `develop`; `.beads/` is tracked), so follow the issue-tracker doc: `br sync --flush-only && git add .beads/` before any commit that touches bead state.
- **Deleted issues persist in `issues.jsonl` as `"status":"tombstone"` rows** (with `deleted_at` / `deleted_by`). This is **correct** — tombstones are how deletions propagate to other clones. Do not try to strip them; `br sync` will refuse, and removing them by hand would let deleted issues resurrect.

## Decisions so far

- [yt-dlp-ejs and pure-JS viability](ytdlp-sab.5): Keep spawning the `yt-dlp` binary — pure-JS (`youtubei.js` and friends) is not durable against YouTube's countermeasures. `yt-dlp-ejs` is a challenge-solver, not a runtime, and is **not needed for subtitles**: verified live that `--write-auto-sub` output is byte-identical (122,555 bytes) with and without a JS runtime. Pass `--js-runtimes node` anyway as free insurance. Report: `archive/research/yt-dlp-js-runtime-and-pure-js-paths.md`

- [Tune the paragraph-break threshold](ytdlp-sab.1): Break at the next sentence end past **100 words**, hard-coded as `PARAGRAPH_MIN_WORDS`. The ticket's premise was falsified — inter-cue gaps are **exactly 0.000s** in all 8 files, so the shipped 2.0s rule has never once fired and 0.8s was equally dead. Word-level timing is speaker-dependent (15/19/125 breaks at one threshold; 696-word worst paragraph); sentence length is stable at 15.5–19.2 words across all 8. The word cap, framed as an optional backstop, turned out to be the primary signal. Transfers to manual subs unchanged. Prototype: branch `prototype/paragraph-rules`.

- [Markdown output and filename contract](ytdlp-sab.2): Slug = NFKD-fold, lowercase, delete apostrophes, non-alphanumeric runs to `-`, trim ends; **120-char** cap truncated at a `-` boundary; empty slug falls back to the video id. Verified against all 8 real titles. Frontmatter is exactly 7 keys in fixed order, with `title`/`channel`/`duration` **always double-quoted** (a bare `duration: 41:18` parses as sexagesimal `2478`; `title: /wayfinder: …` is invalid YAML), `upload_date` as `YYYY-MM-DD`, `fetched` a UTC instant, `url` normalised to `https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=<id>`. Body is plain prose — **no H1, no timestamps**. **Identity is the frontmatter `url`, not the filename**: re-run overwrites silently and bumps `fetched`; a true title collision suffixes the second file with the video id. Re-fetching is **user-driven only** — there is no proactive staleness policy and the catalog, being derived, follows automatically. (This closed the *Transcript freshness* fog patch.)

- [Catalog contents and rebuild semantics](ytdlp-sab.3): The catalog is **`transcripts/README.md`** — the folder README, so the scan rule **"any `.md` with parseable frontmatter is a transcript"** excludes it with no filename special-case. Five columns in order: **Title** (linked to the transcript's relative path), **Channel**, **Duration**, **Uploaded**, **Subtitles**; `url` and `fetched` are deliberately not surfaced. Sort **`upload_date` descending, tie-break `title` ascending** — both immutable, so a re-fetch never reorders a row. Rebuild fires **both** automatically after every successful fetch **and** explicitly via the **`yt-transcript catalog` subcommand** (not a flag, not a second executable), and is **always a full rescan**. **Narrowed by [Playlist and channel handling](ytdlp-sab.4):** the automatic rebuild fires after every successful *single-video* fetch and **once at the end of a batch**, never once per video. Above the table: `# Transcripts`, then `N transcripts, regenerated by yt-transcript catalog`. A malformed transcript is **skipped with a warning naming the file and telling the user to re-download it** — never silent, never fatal. Titles are `|`-escaped in the catalog cell only; zero transcripts yields the count line and no table. **Derivability is the standing acceptance test for any future column:** computable from the seven frontmatter keys plus the file path, or it does not belong.

- [Playlist and channel handling](ytdlp-sab.4): A playlist or channel URL **expands** into a **batch** of fetches; a fetch is still one video, one `yt-dlp` invocation. Detection is **purely syntactic** (yt-dlp picks its extractor by regex before any network I/O), and `watch?v=…&list=…` means **the video** — a deliberate divergence from yt-dlp, which takes the whole playlist, so `--no-playlist` must be passed; `--playlist` forces the batch reading. A bare `@handle` is rewritten to the channel's **Videos tab** (yt-dlp would expand it to Videos + Shorts + Live). **Skipping is batch-only** — a single video URL still overwrites; a batch expands first (2 HTTP requests for 50 items), normalises to the settled `url` form, and subtracts what `transcripts/` already holds, using the same full scan the catalog rebuild performs. `--force` means exactly "ignore the skip set". Failures **continue, collect, report**, exit non-zero if any failed; **HTTP 429 is the one retried exception** (3 attempts, 5s/15s/45s, labelled *rate-limited*), because the no-retry rule was reasoned from permanence. Success requires exit 0 **and** a non-empty subtitle file — a missing language exits 0 silently. Expansion failure is a hard error; zero videos, and an all-skipped batch, are successes. **No cap**, but a **one-second delay between fetches** in batch mode, done by our own loop since every yt-dlp sleep flag acts inside one invocation. **Playlist provenance is not recorded** — the playlist is how you found the video, not what the video is. Evidence: `archive/research/yt-dlp-playlist-and-channel-urls.md`

## Not yet specified

_Nothing. Every remaining question is a live ticket: the last three fog patches graduated when [Playlist and channel handling](ytdlp-sab.4) closed._

## Out of scope

- **Node-manager configuration on this workstation.** Diagnosed during charting: `fnm use system` pointed the fnm multishell junction at a nonexistent sentinel (`Z:\_fnm_\Nothing\Should\Be\Here\installation`) that stayed on PATH, so `yt-dlp` — being Python and walking PATH — died with `WinError 4392`. Fixed at source by changing the profile to `fnm use default`; verified `yt-dlp` then exits 0 with no PATH sanitization. Machine config sits past this map's destination.
- **Non-YouTube sources.**
- **Chunking or embedding transcripts for RAG.**
- **Summarization** — requires an agent, so it is not a human-reproducible workflow, which is the point of this tool.

title: Tune the paragraph-break threshold
description:
## Question

What fixed pause threshold (and word cap, if any) produces readable paragraphs from YouTube auto-generated captions?

The current cleaner breaks a paragraph when the gap between cues exceeds **2.0s**. In practice this almost never fires on auto-captions — they are near-continuous — so the output is one undifferentiated wall of text. Starting point for tuning is **0.8s**.

Resolve by experiment, not by argument: run the cleaner over 2-3 of the existing `.vtt` files at several gap values, show the user real samples side by side, and let them pick. A **fixed time constant** is the deliverable — no runtime heuristics that would require an agent.

Decide also whether a word cap (break after ~N words regardless of timing) is needed as a backstop, or whether a tuned gap alone is sufficient.

**Answer must state:** the chosen constant(s), and whether they are hard-coded or exposed as CLI flags.
close_reason: Resolved: break at next sentence end past 100 words, hard-coded. Cue-pause thresholds proven unusable (gaps are exactly 0.000s in all 8 files).

comments.author: assistant
comments.text:
## Answer

**Rule: break at the next sentence end once the paragraph has reached 100 words. Timing is not used at all.**

```js
const PARAGRAPH_MIN_WORDS = 100;
```

**Hard-coded**, not a CLI flag. The constant proved stable across every speaker tested, so there is nothing for a user to tune, and no flag to document, validate or support.

### The ticket's premise was falsified

The ticket asked for a tuned *pause threshold*, starting at 0.8s. No cue-level pause threshold can ever work: measured across all 8 `.vtt` files in the repo, the gap between consecutive cues is **exactly 0.000s**. YouTube's auto-caption cues are wall-to-wall contiguous by construction (rolling-window captions re-emit the previous line, so each cue starts precisely where the last ended).

Corroborating evidence from production: **every existing `_cleaned.txt` in this repo contains zero blank lines.** The shipped 2.0s rule has never fired once. 0.8s would have been equally dead.

### Why punctuation, not word-level timing

Word-level timings *do* exist (the inline `<00:00:02.560>` markers) and were evaluated. They are speaker-dependent and unreliable:

| Candidate | paragraphs (3 videos) | mean words | longest paragraph |
|---|---|---|---|
| Current (2.0s cue pause) | 1 / 1 / 1 | 2486 / 2258 / 7214 | — one wall of text |
| Word pause >= 1.0s | 15 / 19 / 125 | 166 / 119 / 58 | **696** |
| **Sentence end + 100 words** | **22 / 21 / 64** | **113 / 108 / 113** | **141 / 141 / 160** |
| Sentence end + 60 words | 36 / 33 / 102 | 69 / 68 / 71 | 97 / 103 / 142 |
| Sentence end + 150 words | 16 / 14 / 45 | 155 / 161 / 160 | 178 / 172 / 216 |
| Hybrid (40 words or 0.8s) | 54 / 49 / 169 | 46 / 46 / 43 | 73 / 68 / 123 |

The same timing threshold yields 15, 19 and 125 breaks on three videos, and still leaves 696-word walls. Sentence length, by contrast, is **15.5–19.2 words in all 8 files** — the most stable quantity in the data.

**The punctuation is YouTube's, not ours.** The raw VTT payload is `Skills,<c> skills,</c><c> skills.</c><c> Folks,</c>` — YouTube's ASR emits capitalisation and sentence punctuation. `clean-transcript.js` never inserts a period.

This **inverts the ticket's framing**: the word cap, offered as an optional backstop to a tuned gap, is the primary signal, and timing is dropped entirely. The constraint the ticket actually cared about — a fixed constant, no runtime heuristics needing an agent — is fully honoured.

**Bonus: this transfers to manually-authored subtitles unchanged.** Human-written subs are punctuated by construction but are *not* rolling-window, so a timing rule would have needed a second variant for them. A punctuation-gated word cap needs none.

### Detection rule

A word ends a sentence when it matches `/[.!?]["')\]]?$/`. This false-fires on abbreviations (`etc.`, `Dr.`), which can only end a paragraph slightly early, and only once past the 100-word gate — bounded, and the measured maxima (~1.4x target) confirm it is not pathological. Not worth an abbreviation list.

### Implementation note for the spec

The paragraph splitter needs word-level tokens, but `clean-transcript.js`'s dedup (`getOverlapSize`) discards timings. The prototype ports that dedup onto `{word, onset}` tokens and **verifies the result is identical to `processTranscript` on all 8 files**. Since the chosen rule needs no timings, the implementer may keep plain strings — but the verified parser is on the branch either way.

Also found: `clean-transcript.js` runs its CLI block at module scope, so merely importing it writes a file. The spec must require an entry guard.

### Prototype

Branch `prototype/paragraph-rules` (commit `702d396`) — `.scratch/para/`:
- `words-parse.mjs` — dedup ported onto timed tokens
- `verify.mjs` — proves it matches `processTranscript` on all 8 files
- `rules.mjs`, `build.mjs` — the six candidates
- `paragraph-rules.prototype.html` — the side-by-side the user picked from

comments.text:
## Confirmation across all 8 transcripts

The table above reports the chosen rule on 3 sample videos. Re-run over **all 8** `.vtt` files in the repo, `PARAGRAPH_MIN_WORDS = 100` holds:

| Transcript | words | paragraphs | mean | max |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4JofSJIrjwU | 9388 | 86 | 109 | 146 |
| F3lL98Pj90o | 3144 | 29 | 108 | 131 |
| gaDdrDdczO4 | 2486 | 22 | 113 | 141 |
| hfba9dAT6xE | 7965 | 73 | 109 | 143 |
| LoMOPj-lO8U | 3379 | 31 | 109 | 140 |
| M6mYodf0dJM | 3717 | 35 | 106 | 121 |
| n0VhIVtviC0 | 2258 | 21 | 108 | 141 |
| o3CX_Y59_74 | 7214 | 64 | 113 | 160 |

**Mean 106–113 words in every file; longest paragraph anywhere is 160.** Since the rule breaks at the first sentence end past 100 words, the worst case is bounded by `100 + longest sentence`; no unpunctuated stretch in the corpus pushes it beyond 1.6x the target. The claim generalises.

title: Markdown output and filename contract
description:
## Question

What exactly does a transcript file look like, and what is it called?

**Filename.** Kebab-case of the video title. The edge cases are real and present in this repo already: an en-dash, a title beginning with `--`, and the general problem of emoji, `|`, `:`, `?`, `/`, and non-ASCII characters. Decide the slug algorithm, whether there is a length cap, and what happens on **collision** (two videos, one title).

**Body.** YAML frontmatter carrying `title`, `url`, `duration`, `fetched`, `channel`, `upload_date`, `subtitles` (`manual` | `auto`), followed by the cleaned transcript. Decide whether the title is repeated as an H1, whether paragraphs are plain or carry timestamps, and anything else the body needs to be useful as agent input.

**Re-runs.** Requesting a video that already has a transcript: overwrite, skip, or error?

**Answer must state:** the slug algorithm precisely enough to implement, the exact frontmatter key set and value formats, the body layout, and the re-run policy.
close_reason: Transcript file contract settled: slug algorithm + 120-char cap + video-id fallback, seven-key frontmatter with explicit value formats, plain-prose body with no H1 or timestamps, and URL-based identity with silent overwrite on re-run.

comments.author: assistant
comments.text:
## Answer: the transcript file contract

### Filename

One file per video in flat `transcripts/`, extension `.md`.

**Slug algorithm**, applied to the video title, in order:

1. Unicode-normalise NFKD and strip combining marks (diacritics folded to ASCII).
2. Lowercase.
3. **Delete** apostrophes and quote marks (`'`, `’`, `"`, `“`, `”`) outright — no separator. `Don't` → `dont`, not `don-t`.
4. Replace every remaining run of characters outside `[a-z0-9]` with a single `-`.
5. Trim leading and trailing `-`.

No special cases. Step 5 is what disposes of the `--` prefix and the leading `/` in `/wayfinder:` without special-casing either. `&` falls out as a separator (`Build & Deploy` → `build-deploy`); dots are separators too, so `v1.2` → `v1-2` and `INTENT.MD` → `intent-md`.

**Length cap: 120 characters**, truncated at the last `-` boundary at or before 120, trailing `-` trimmed. The full title is never lost — it is in the frontmatter.

**Empty slug** (title is entirely non-Latin — Greek, Japanese, Cyrillic — or pure emoji/punctuation): fall back to the **video id** as the filename, e.g. `o3CX_Y59_74.md`. No transliteration dependency.

**Verified test vector** — the eight videos already in this repo, with live yt-dlp titles:

| title | slug |
|---|---|
| How to Fine-Tune any AI Model Locally (FULL Tutorial) | `how-to-fine-tune-any-ai-model-locally-full-tutorial` |
| /wayfinder: Nothing is too big to plan anymore | `wayfinder-nothing-is-too-big-to-plan-anymore` |
| New Skills! v1.2 brings /wait-what, /writing-for-agents, and fixes /grill-me | `new-skills-v1-2-brings-wait-what-writing-for-agents-and-fixes-grill-me` |
| The Best LOCAL Agentic Coding Workflow (Complete Guide) | `the-best-local-agentic-coding-workflow-complete-guide` |
| Claude Codes New INTENT.MD, What is It? | `claude-codes-new-intent-md-what-is-it` |
| mattpocock/skills: A complete AI Coding workflow, end-to-end | `mattpocock-skills-a-complete-ai-coding-workflow-end-to-end` |
| Don't waste time on specs: /prototype instead | `dont-waste-time-on-specs-prototype-instead` |
| OpenAI Codex Crash Course – Build & Deploy Apps with Autonomous AI | `openai-codex-crash-course-build-deploy-apps-with-autonomous-ai` |

These eight are the implementer's test cases: they cover a leading `/`, an en-dash, a `&`, an apostrophe, dots inside a version number and inside `INTENT.MD`, parentheses, `!`, `?`, and commas.

### Frontmatter

Exactly seven keys, in this order:

```yaml
---
title: "OpenAI Codex Crash Course – Build & Deploy Apps with Autonomous AI"
url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o3CX_Y59_74
channel: "freeCodeCamp.org"
duration: "41:18"
upload_date: 2026-09-10
fetched: 2026-09-16T14:03:05Z
subtitles: auto
---
```

Value formats, all deliberate:

- **`title`** and **`channel`**: **always** double-quoted, with `\` and `"` escaped. Unconditional, not quote-when-needed. Three of the eight titles contain a `:` and one begins with `/`; `title: /wayfinder: Nothing is too big...` is invalid YAML. A conditional rule is one an implementer gets subtly wrong.
- **`url`**: normalised to `https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=<id>` regardless of input form (`youtu.be/`, `/shorts/`, bare id, `?si=`/`&t=` junk). One shape on disk, one regex to read it back. Safe bare.
- **`duration`**: **always double-quoted** — `duration: 41:18` unquoted is *not a string*; YAML 1.1 parsers read colon-separated digits as a sexagesimal integer and yield `2478`, and parsers disagree with each other about it. Format is `M:SS`, widening to `H:MM:SS` only once the video passes an hour. No zero-padding on the leading unit, matching how YouTube itself displays durations.
- **`upload_date`**: reformatted from yt-dlp's native `20260910` to `2026-09-10`. A bare `20260910` is a number-shaped string that YAML parsers and humans both misread.
- **`fetched`**: full ISO-8601 **UTC** instant, `Z`-suffixed. A date alone loses same-day re-fetches, and freshness is the whole point of the field.
- **`subtitles`**: `manual` or `auto`, bare.

No `video_id` key — `url` carries it.

### Body

Immediately after the closing `---`: the cleaned transcript as plain prose paragraphs separated by blank lines. **No H1** (the title is in the frontmatter; repeating it is redundant for the agent that consumes this) and **no per-paragraph timestamps** (noise in prose, and the paragraphing decision already established that this pipeline's timing data is unusable). Paragraphs break per `PARAGRAPH_MIN_WORDS = 100` at the next sentence end.

### Identity and re-runs

**Identity is the frontmatter `url`, never the filename.** A transcript for video X exists **iff** some file in `transcripts/` has a frontmatter `url` whose video id is X.

This matters because the slug alone cannot distinguish "re-fetch of the same video" from "different video that happens to share a title". The scan costs nothing new — the catalog is derived by reading every transcript's frontmatter anyway.

- **Re-run of the same video** → **overwrite in place, silently**, and bump `fetched`. A transcript is derived data; re-fetching is precisely how you pick up improved auto-captions.
- **Different video, same slug** → the *second* file gains a video-id suffix: `same-title-<videoid>.md`. Only the loser of the collision is uglified; the common case stays clean.

**This is the definition ticket _Playlist and channel handling_ needs for "already fetched":** a catalog/frontmatter `url` lookup, not a filename match.

comments.author: assistant
comments.text:
## Addendum: the slug rule drops non-Latin letters silently

The empty-slug fallback above covers a title that slugifies to **nothing**. Reviewing the algorithm against mixed-script and Latin-extended titles exposed a worse case it does *not* cover.

**Mixed script.** `Νέα Skills! v1.2 για agents` → the Greek letters carry no combining marks, so NFKD leaves them intact, and step 4 turns each run into a separator. Result: `skills-v1-2`. Non-empty, so the video-id fallback never fires — and the filename has silently swallowed most of the title while looking perfectly plausible. That is strictly worse than `o3CX_Y59_74.md`, which at least announces that it gave up.

**Latin-extended.** The same mechanism, one character at a time: `Søren` → `s-ren`, `Paweł` → `pawe-`, `Straße` → `stra-e`. No combining mark to strip, so a letter becomes punctuation.

### Refinement

Two additions, both inside the existing algorithm — nothing else about the contract changes:

1. **Between steps 2 and 3, transliterate the Latin letters NFKD does not decompose**, via a small fixed table: `ø→o`, `ł→l`, `đ→d`, `ß→ss`, `æ→ae`, `œ→oe`, `þ→th`, `ð→d`. This fixes the Latin-extended case properly rather than giving up on it: `soren`, `pawel`, `strasse`.

2. **After step 5, compute a retention ratio**: alphanumeric characters in the slug, divided by Unicode letters-plus-digits in the original title. **If retention is below 50%, discard the slug and use the video id as the filename.**

Rule 2 subsumes the empty-slug case (retention 0%), so it replaces that clause rather than sitting beside it. Under it, `Νέα Skills! v1.2 για agents` retains roughly 30% and correctly falls back to the id; all eight titles in the verified test vector retain 100% and are unaffected.

Rationale: a filename is a convenience, and a *misleading* convenience is worth less than an honest video id. The frontmatter `title` and the catalog both carry the real title regardless, and identity rests on the frontmatter `url`, so a fallback filename costs nothing functional.

title: Catalog contents and rebuild semantics
description:
## Question

What is in the catalog, and how is it rebuilt?

A Markdown file, **derived** from the frontmatter of the files in `transcripts/` so it cannot drift from reality.

Decide: where it lives (`transcripts/README.md`, repo root, elsewhere); which columns it carries and in what order; how it sorts; whether it links to each transcript by relative path; and how rebuild is triggered — automatically after every fetch, via an explicit flag on the single entry point, or both.

Constraint from the user: no script calling another script, and no proliferation of scripts. Rebuild is a mode of the one CLI, not a second executable.

**Answer must state:** the catalog's path, its exact column set, sort order, and the rebuild trigger.
close_reason: Catalog is transcripts/README.md; five derived columns; upload_date desc; rebuild both automatic and via the yt-transcript catalog subcommand, always a full rescan.

comments.author: assistant
comments.text:
## Answer

**Path:** `transcripts/README.md`. It is the folder's front door, renders automatically when the directory is opened, and sits next to what it is derived from. The rebuild scans the directory containing its own output, so the scan rule is **"any `.md` with parseable frontmatter is a transcript"** — the README has none and is excluded as a side effect, with no filename special-case.

**Columns** (exact set, exact order):

| Column | Source | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Title | `title` | Hyperlinked to the transcript's relative path |
| Channel | `channel` | |
| Duration | `duration` | Rendered as stored |
| Uploaded | `upload_date` | `YYYY-MM-DD` |
| Subtitles | `subtitles` | `manual` or `auto` |

Two frontmatter keys are deliberately **not** surfaced: `url` (the Title already links onward into the transcript, and the YouTube URL is one step further in, in the file's own frontmatter) and `fetched` (provenance, not something you browse by — and including it would churn a table row on every re-fetch).

Every column is computable from the seven frontmatter keys plus the file's own path. That is the acceptance test for any future column: if it is not derivable from those, it does not belong in the catalog, because admitting it would either reopen the closed frontmatter contract or reintroduce exactly the drift the catalog exists to prevent.

**Sort:** `upload_date` **descending**, tie-break `title` **ascending**. Both keys are immutable, so a re-fetch never reorders a row. Sorting by `fetched` was rejected for precisely that churn; alphabetical-by-title was rejected because a library of talks reads best newest-first.

**Rebuild trigger: both.** Automatically after every **successful** fetch, and explicitly via `yt-transcript catalog`. Automatic-only goes stale the moment a transcript is deleted or hand-edited outside the tool — which is exactly when an index starts lying. Explicit-only makes the common path two commands.

`catalog` is a **subcommand** on the single entry point, not a flag, and not a second executable. `yt-transcript <url|id>` remains the bare default. The reasoning: rebuild takes no target and does something categorically different from fetching, which is what a verb slot is for; a second mode-flag later would fight the first.

Rebuild is **always a full rescan**, never an incremental append. That is what makes drift structurally impossible rather than merely unlikely.

**Above the table:** an `# Transcripts` H1, then a single line — `N transcripts, regenerated by ` + `yt-transcript catalog` — then the table. The regeneration note is load-bearing: the file is derived, so anyone hand-editing it loses the edit on the next fetch and the file must say so. The count is free and makes an incomplete rebuild visible at a glance.

**Malformed transcript:** a `.md` whose frontmatter is unparseable or missing required keys is **skipped with a warning** naming the file and telling the user to re-download it. Not silent — a transcript vanishing from the index with no signal is the precise failure a derived catalog exists to prevent. Not fatal — one bad file should not cost you the whole catalog.

## Consequences settled here

- **Stub rows are impossible by construction.** The catalog is a pure function of the directory, so it cannot hold a row for a video with no transcript file. This **constrains** the open *No subtitles at all* question: "record a stub in the catalog" is only reachable by writing a real transcript file with real frontmatter. That remains that ticket's call; the constraint is recorded, the fog patch is not resolved.
- **Pipe escaping.** A `|` in a video title would break the Markdown table row, so titles are escaped as `\|` **in the catalog cell only**. The frontmatter and filename contracts are untouched.
- **Empty state.** Zero transcripts yields the H1 and a `0 transcripts` line with no table, rather than an empty table skeleton.

## Deferred, not decided

Whether the catalog records **playlist membership** belongs to *Playlist and channel handling* and was deliberately not settled here. Note for that ticket: any playlist column must pass the derivability test above, which today it fails — playlist provenance is not among the seven frontmatter keys, so recording it means amending the frontmatter contract, not just the catalog.

## No ADR

Path, column set and sort are all cheap to reverse and unsurprising. The rebuild trigger is the expected answer rather than a contested trade-off. None of the three ADR criteria is met.

comments.author: assistant
comments.text:
## Amended by Playlist and channel handling (ytdlp-sab.4)

This ticket settled that a rebuild fires automatically **after every successful fetch**. That rule is
now narrowed: after every successful **single-video** fetch, and **once at the end of a batch** — not
once per video, which would make a 200-video playlist run quadratic.

Everything else here stands unchanged: the rebuild is still always a full rescan, still also available
explicitly via `yt-transcript catalog`, and the catalog is still derived wholly from frontmatter.

Accepted consequence: a batch interrupted part-way leaves transcripts on disk that the catalog does not
yet list, until `yt-transcript catalog` is run. Because the catalog is derived and rebuilt by full
rescan, that state can only ever be incomplete, never wrong.

Also decided there, and relevant to this ticket: playlist provenance is **not** recorded, so the seven
frontmatter keys and the five catalog columns are unchanged by playlist support.

title: Playlist and channel handling
description:
## Question

What happens when the user hands `yt-transcript` a playlist or channel URL?

Playlist and channel support is in scope; the single entry point detects a playlist itself rather than delegating to a separate script.

Decide: how a playlist/channel URL is distinguished from a video URL; whether already-fetched videos are skipped (and what "already fetched" means — filename match, or catalog lookup); what happens when one video in a batch fails (abort, continue-and-report, retry); whether there is a cap or rate limit; and whether the catalog records playlist membership at all.

**Answer must state:** the detection rule, the skip rule, the partial-failure policy, and whether playlist provenance is recorded.
close_reason: Resolved: detection is syntactic and video-wins on list=; skip is batch-only keyed on frontmatter url; continue-and-report with a named 429 exception; no provenance recorded.

comments.author: assistant
comments.text:
## Resolution

A playlist or channel URL **expands** into a **batch** of fetches. Each fetch is still one video, one
`yt-dlp` invocation; the batch is the only new unit.

### Detection rule — purely syntactic, no network call

Verified: yt-dlp selects its extractor by regex before any network I/O, so URL shape alone decides.

- `watch?v=<id>` (with or without `&si=`/`&t=` junk), `youtu.be/<id>`, `/shorts/<id>`, bare id → **one video**.
- `/playlist?list=<id>` → **batch**.
- `youtube.com/@handle`, `/c/Name`, `/channel/UC…` → **batch**, rewritten to the channel's **Videos tab**.
- `watch?v=<id>&list=<listid>` → **one video**. `list=` is discarded like other trailing junk;
  `--playlist` forces the batch reading.

Two divergences from `yt-dlp` that must be implemented deliberately, not inherited:

1. yt-dlp's default on `watch?v=&list=` is the **opposite** — it takes the whole playlist. We must pass
   `--no-playlist`. A URL carrying `v=` names a video: that is what the user copied from the address bar
   while watching, and the playlist tail is an artifact of how they arrived. Deliberate playlist intent
   has its own URL form; accidental playlist intent costs 200 downloads.
2. A bare `@handle` expands in yt-dlp to **Videos + Shorts + Live** as three sub-playlists (verified on a
   real channel). We rewrite it to the Videos tab. A 45-second Short is not a video you have no time to
   watch, and a livestream's auto-captions are mostly silence. `@handle/shorts` and `@handle/streams`
   are still honoured when named explicitly — the narrowing applies only to the ambiguous bare form.

### Skip rule — expand first, batch only

- **Single video URL: never skipped.** The settled overwrite-always behaviour from *Markdown output and
  filename contract* is untouched. Naming one video is a command; you meant it.
- **Batch: skipped by default.** The URL list is obtained by a flat expansion
  (`--flat-playlist --simulate --print`), normalised to the settled `https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=<id>`
  form, and subtracted from the URLs already present in `transcripts/` frontmatter. Only the remainder is
  fetched, so the skip saves the download, not merely the file write.
- Identity is the frontmatter `url`, never the filename — inherited unchanged.
- The known-URL set comes from the **same full scan of `transcripts/` that the catalog rebuild performs**.
  One scan implementation, two callers.
- `--force` has exactly one meaning: **ignore the skip set**. On a single video URL it is accepted and is
  a silent no-op, so scripts may pass it uniformly. There is no `--no-playlist` counterpart flag.
- Expansion is cheap enough to make this the obvious order: a 50-item playlist costs **2 HTTP requests**,
  200 items costs 7.

### Partial-failure policy — continue, collect, report

- A failed video never stops the batch. Each failure is collected with its reason and printed in a summary
  at the end, naming the video — mirroring the catalog's settled "skipped with a warning naming the file"
  posture. Never silent, never fatal.
- **No general retry layer.** yt-dlp already retries network faults, and our failures are mostly permanent:
  deleted, private, members-only, region-blocked.
- **HTTP 429 is the one named exception**, because it is transient and retrying is the correct response.
  Three attempts, backing off 5s / 15s / 45s, then the video enters the failure summary labelled
  *rate-limited* — distinct from other reasons, because it tells the user to re-run later rather than to
  give up. This is not a hole in the no-retry rule; the rule was reasoned from permanence, and a rate-limit
  response is not permanent.
- **Exit non-zero if any video failed**, so a scripted run cannot quietly under-deliver.
- **Success is exit code 0 AND a non-empty subtitle file on disk.** Exit code alone is insufficient:
  requesting a subtitle language that does not exist exits **0 with no error line and no file** (verified).
  A file that arrives but cleans to nothing is a cleaner bug — loud and separate, not a fetch failure.
- Because we expand ourselves and invoke yt-dlp once per video, exit codes are per-video and unambiguous.
  yt-dlp's own inability to distinguish "all failed" from "some failed" via exit code never reaches us.

### Batch-level failure, as distinct from failure within a batch

- **Expansion failure is a hard error**: private playlist, deleted channel, mistyped handle. No batch
  starts, non-zero exit, no catalog rebuild.
- **Zero videos returned is not an error** — reports `0 videos`, exits 0.
- **A batch where every video is already fetched is a success** — reports
  `47 videos, 47 already fetched, nothing to do`, exits 0.
- The line is whether we failed to *learn what the URL names*, versus learning it names nothing new.

### Rate limiting — a delay, not a cap

- **No cap on batch size.** Any number would defend an unquantified threshold: it would block legitimate
  use without guaranteeing safety.
- **A fixed one-second delay between fetches in batch mode**, implemented by our own batch loop; the
  single-video path is untouched. This is deliberately *not* a yt-dlp flag: because we expand ourselves
  and spawn yt-dlp once per video, `--sleep-requests` (sleeps between requests *during extraction*) and
  `--sleep-interval` / `--sleep-subtitles` (sleep *before* a download) all act **inside** a single
  invocation and cannot space one spawn from the next. Only the caller can do that. (Implementer note,
  not a decision: `--sleep-requests` was purpose-built for exactly this throttling problem — yt-dlp #106
  — so it remains the first lever to reach for if one-second spacing proves insufficient.)
- The risk is specific to us, not hypothetical: yt-dlp's sleep flags all **default to off**, and yt-dlp
  issue **#13831** is an open report of **429s on auto-generated subtitle requests** — the exact call a
  batch makes hundreds of times. A maintainer records that an earlier fix held only "for a while" before
  YouTube tightened further, and no workaround is reliable. No one cites a volume threshold, which is
  precisely why a numeric cap would be theatre and a one-second sleep is the only lever with evidence
  behind it.

### Playlist provenance — not recorded

A transcript does not remember the playlist it arrived via. The frontmatter stays **exactly seven keys**,
and the catalog gains no column. Three reasons: it would break a settled contract; playlist membership is
not a property of the video (one video sits in many playlists, and membership changes after the fetch, so
the field would rot); and `channel` already answers the question people actually ask. **The playlist is how
you found the video, not what the video is.**

`playlist_id` / `playlist_title` / `playlist_index` / `playlist_uploader` are all reliably available from
yt-dlp and are deliberately discarded. (`playlist_count` is `NA` on channel tabs, so a progress total on a
channel must come from our own expansion, not from that field.)

### Catalog rebuild — amends *Catalog contents and rebuild semantics*

That ticket settled "rebuild fires automatically after every successful fetch." **This narrows it:** after
every successful *single-video* fetch, and **once at the end of a batch** — not once per video, which would
make a 200-video run quadratic.

**Accepted consequence:** a batch interrupted by `Ctrl-C` or a crash leaves transcripts on disk that the
catalog does not list, until someone runs `yt-transcript catalog`. The catalog remains derived and a full
rescan, so the remedy is always one command and can never produce a wrong result — only a briefly
incomplete one.

### Ordering and output

- Fetches run in **playlist order as yt-dlp returns it**: the creator's intended order, stable across runs,
  so an interrupted batch resumes predictably. Fetch order does not affect the catalog, whose sort is
  settled independently as `upload_date` descending.
- A batch prints an **expansion line** up front (total / already fetched / to fetch), **one line per video**
  as it completes (index, count, title, and whether manual or auto subtitles were used), and the **failure
  summary** at the end.
- The single-video path prints that same per-video line. A batch is a fetch repeated, so it gets no display
  language of its own; `1/1` reads fine.

### CLI surface after this ticket

```
yt-transcript <video-url|id>          one fetch, overwrites
yt-transcript <playlist-url>          batch, skips already-fetched
yt-transcript <channel-url>           batch over the Videos tab
yt-transcript catalog                 full rescan (settled previously)
  --playlist                          force the batch reading of watch?v=...&list=...
  --force                             ignore the skip set (no-op on a single video)
```

### Glossary

`CONTEXT.md` gained **Batch** and **Expand**, and **Fetch** was tightened to exactly one video —
a playlist is many fetches, never one large one.

### Deliberately not decided here

**What the CLI does when a video has no captions at all** in the requested language. This ticket settles
only how a fetch *detects* that condition so a batch can report it; the policy — hard error, or fall back to
another language — graduates to its own ticket.

Evidence for every yt-dlp behavioural claim above: `archive/research/yt-dlp-playlist-and-channel-urls.md`.

title: yt-dlp-ejs and pure-JS viability
description:
## Question

Is `yt-dlp-ejs` usable in our case, and is a pure-JavaScript transcript pipeline durable enough to replace the `yt-dlp` binary?

Running `yt-dlp` today emits a deprecation warning: no supported JavaScript runtime found, only Deno enabled by default, "YouTube extraction without a JS runtime has been deprecated". Two things to establish:

1. **yt-dlp-ejs** (https://github.com/yt-dlp/ejs) — what it is, whether Node can serve as the runtime instead of Deno and with what `--js-runtimes` syntax, whether it must be installed separately, whether the warning affects **subtitle downloads** specifically or only media format extraction, and whether there is a deadline after which extraction breaks.
2. **Pure-JS alternatives** — whether any maintained npm package reliably fetches auto-generated captions, metadata, and playlists against current YouTube bot-detection, with evidence from recent issues rather than marketing copy.

The user's preference rule is settled: **robustness wins.** Pure-JS is adopted only if it is durable, not merely possible. The expected outcome is confirmation that spawning `yt-dlp` is correct, plus a concrete answer on whether to pass `--js-runtimes` to silence/avoid the deprecation.

**Answer must state:** whether ejs is usable here, whether the warning matters for subtitles, and the final fetching architecture.
close_reason: Resolved: spawn yt-dlp binary; pure-JS not durable; --js-runtimes node as insurance. Subtitle immunity verified live (byte-identical output).

comments.author: assistant
comments.text:
## Answer

**Keep spawning the `yt-dlp` binary. Pure-JS is not durable. `yt-dlp-ejs` is not needed for our case, but pass `--js-runtimes node` as cheap insurance.**

### Is ejs usable here?

`yt-dlp-ejs` is a **challenge-solver script package, not a runtime**. It solves YouTube's n/signature and BotGuard-style JS challenges inside a separate JS engine that yt-dlp invokes. Node **is** officially supported via `--js-runtimes node` (minimum v22; this machine runs v24), but it is second-tier — Deno is the only first-class default and silently wins if both are installed, so forcing Node where Deno also exists needs `--no-js-runtimes --js-runtimes node`. The ejs component ships bundled in official yt-dlp executables.

### Does the warning affect subtitles? — **Verified live: no.**

The research flagged this as unresolved, inferring from yt-dlp's PO Token Guide (which lists "Subs" as its own PO-Token-gated case) that subtitle fetches might be affected. Reproduced directly instead, on this machine, against `gaDdrDdczO4`:

| Run | Command | Result |
|---|---|---|
| A | `--write-auto-sub --sub-lang en --skip-download` | `gaDdrDdczO4.en.vtt` — **122,555 bytes** |
| B | `--js-runtimes node --write-auto-sub --sub-lang en --skip-download` | `gaDdrDdczO4.en.vtt` — **122,555 bytes** |

Identical size, and identical to the copy already in the repo. The deprecation warning is **cosmetic for our use case today**: auto-caption downloads do not currently need a JS runtime. `--js-runtimes node` is accepted without error and suppresses the warning.

No formal deadline for a hard break has been announced — only an open-ended "expected to worsen" statement. Hard failures already occur today for logged-in and age-gated content, neither of which we touch.

### Pure-JS alternatives — not viable

- `ytdl-core`: unmaintained since 2023.
- `@distube/ytdl-core`: repository archived; its own README redirects users to `youtubei.js`.
- `youtubei.js`: the only actively maintained full-featured candidate, but rides the same YouTube-chasing treadmill as yt-dlp, with recent bot-detection/403 issues, and does not solve PoToken generation itself.
- Transcript-only scrapers (`youtube-transcript`, `youtube-captions-scraper`): no PoToken handling, documented IP-banning failures by design.

Replacing yt-dlp with any of these trades a tool maintained specifically to survive YouTube's countermeasures for one that is not. Against the settled preference rule — robustness wins — that trade fails.

### Architecture, settled

Node CLI spawns the `yt-dlp` binary as a child process. Preflight-check for `yt-dlp` on PATH and fail with a clear, actionable message if absent. Pass `--js-runtimes node` on every invocation: it costs nothing, silences the deprecation warning, and means the pipeline keeps working on the day subtitles *do* start requiring a runtime.

### Caveats carried forward

The verification above is a single video at a single point in time. If auto-captions ever come back empty or truncated, `--js-runtimes node` is already in place, and the next thing to check is PO Token requirements for the `web` client.

Full research report with citations: `docs/research/yt-dlp-js-runtime-and-pure-js-paths.md`

comments.author: assistant
comments.text:
**Correction — research report relocated.**

The report has moved from `docs/research/` to **`archive/research/yt-dlp-js-runtime-and-pure-js-paths.md`**.

Rationale: `CLAUDE.md` designates `archive/` for notes and research materials, while `docs/` is reserved for normative project documentation (`CONTEXT.md`, `docs/adr/`, `docs/agents/`). A research report is the evidence behind a decision, not the decision itself — when this one is distilled into an ADR, that ADR is the normative artifact and cites the archived report.

title: Missing subtitles in the requested language
description:
## Question

What does `yt-transcript` do when a video has **no subtitles at all** in the requested language —
neither manually-authored nor auto-generated?

Hard error, or fall back to another language?

**Constrained by decisions already made:**

- The catalog is a pure function of `transcripts/`, so a bare "stub row in the catalog" is not
  reachable. Remembering such a video at all requires writing a real transcript file with real
  frontmatter — and the `subtitles` frontmatter key is settled as exactly `manual | auto`, with no
  third value.
- *Playlist and channel handling* settled the **detection** rule but deliberately not the policy:
  a fetch succeeded only if yt-dlp exited 0 **and** a non-empty subtitle file exists. Requesting a
  language that does not exist exits **0 with no error line and no file** (verified), so this
  condition is detectable but currently has no defined response.
- In a batch the video lands in the failure summary. The open question is what happens on the
  **single-video** path, and whether "no captions in `en`" should silently become "captions in `es`".

**Answer must state:** the single-video behaviour, the batch behaviour, whether any language
fallback happens and if so how the chosen language is surfaced to the user, and the exit code.

title: Dedup safety on manually-authored subtitles
description:
## Question

Does the cleaner's `getOverlapSize` dedup step corrupt **manually-authored** subtitles?

The dedup logic assumes the rolling-window repetition that YouTube's auto-generated captions produce,
where each cue restates the tail of the previous one. Manual subtitles have no rolling window, so a
genuinely repeated phrase — "Yes. Yes.", a chorus, a deliberate restatement — could be silently
collapsed into one.

This matters now because manual subtitles are the **preferred** track, so this is the path taken
whenever it is available, and a silent deletion of real speech is exactly the failure a transcript
must not have.

Worth resolving with a prototype against real manual-subtitle input rather than by reading the code:
the question is empirical.

**Answer must state:** whether the corruption is real and under what input, and whether dedup is
skipped entirely on manual tracks, applied with different parameters, or left as-is with evidence
that it is safe.

title: Shape and granularity of the spec hand-off
description:
## Question

What shape and granularity should the final hand-off take, so that **one implementer session** can
build `yt-transcript` end to end?

Every contract decision is now settled — fetching, output and filename, frontmatter, paragraphing,
catalog, playlist and channel handling. What remains is deciding how to present them.

Decide: whether the hand-off is a single spec ticket or several; how much of each closed ticket's
reasoning is restated versus linked; whether `CONTEXT.md` and the agent procedure doc are prerequisites
of the spec or products of the build; which decisions warrant an ADR (the bar being hard to reverse,
surprising without context, and the result of a real trade-off — the `watch?v=&list=` divergence from
yt-dlp's own default and the deliberate rejection of pure-JS fetching are the obvious candidates); and
what the implementer is expected to have on disk before starting.

Note the existing-artifact migration (7 `.vtt` files and their cleaned siblings at the repo root, plus
strays) is hand-off execution, not a decision — but the hand-off must say who does it and when.

**Answer must state:** the hand-off artifact list, what each contains, and which ADRs get written.
